reply: We propose a first‐stage laboratory comparison using a combined ATR‑MIR probe and a fluorimetric probe at the same tip, measuring the same tissue spot and building separate and fused classification models. The experiment will show whether the concatenated MIR‑ATR and fluorescence data improve tissue‑type separation beyond each method alone.

report.title: MIR‑ATR + Fluorescence comparison on model tissues

answer.text: It depends on whether the combined MIR‑ATR and fluorescence data provide complementary information for classification; the first experiment will test that hypothesis.

concept.summary: Use a single multispectral probe that integrates an ATR crystal for MIR absorption and a side‑view fluorimetric fiber for absorption/detection; place the probe in contact with the tissue surface; route the fibers to a benchtop MIR spectrometer and a fluorometer; acquire spectra sequentially (sub‑second delay) from the same spot; build separate PCA/PLS‑DA models and a fused model by concatenating the data matrices.
concept.probe: ATR crystal tip with co‑located fluorimetric fiber (as in the combined probe of S04.2.1)
concept.location: In‑line with the sample holder (e.g., on a translation stage) so the same spot can be measured by both modalities
concept.fiberLink: Standard silica fiber for fluorescence (visible range) and chalcogenide fiber for MIR (4000‑400 cm⁻¹) as demonstrated in S04.1.6
concept.analyzer: Benchtop MIR FT‑IR spectrometer (ATR mode) plus a bench‑top fluorometer; data streamed to a PC for chemometric fusion

risks: ATR sampling depth is only a few microns; may not represent bulk tissue heterogeneity.
Fluorescence signal can be weak for some tissues and may be affected by scattering.
Sequential acquisition could still sample slightly different micro‑areas if tissue is highly heterogeneous.

steps: Prepare at least three independent samples of each tissue type (muscle, fat, liver) as in.
Measure each sample with the combined probe, recording MIR‑ATR and fluorescence spectra from the same spot.
Preprocess spectra (baseline correction, normalization) and build separate classification models (e.g., PCA‑DA).
Concatenate the two data blocks and build a fused model; validate on held‑out samples not used for training.
Compare classification accuracy of single‑method models versus the fused model to assess the benefit of combination.
Then measure fresh specimens under realistic conditions against the reference method.
feasibility.decisionBasis: If the fused model shows a statistically significant improvement in class separation (e.g., higher correct classification rate) over the single‑method models, the combination is justified for further development. Agree two things separately with the customer before the test: the model accuracy required against the reference method, and the alarm or action threshold applied to the measured value.
